transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
And approaching Hurricane East IES is prompting evacuations and school closures along the
U.S. Gulf Coast.
Michael Brennan, the director of the National Hurricane Center, is tracking this storm.
The hurricane is going to make landfall somewhere along the north-central Gulf Coast late Friday
night into the early morning hours on Saturday.
We are expecting ECS to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall.
We have hurricane warnings in effect for portions of the Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida Gulf
Coast from Ocean Springs over through Bay County, Florida.
In addition to heavy rainfall and floods, the storm also threatens to generate tornadoes
overnight Friday to Saturday.
A federal judge is expected to decide by next Tuesday whether to extend an earlier order
restoring White House access for journalists from Politico, CNN, and MSNow.
Today, an attorney for the three media organizations arguing in court that the Trump administration's
actions are a classic example of "viewpoint discrimination" and it should be blocked from
imposing the ban.
President Trump has said the outlet's coverage of him has been persistently inaccurate and
unfair.
But today, the Justice Department again raised national security concerns with the media
organization's coverage.
The Justice Department has brought a new indictment against former Venezuelan president, Nicolas
Maduro, and his wife.
The couple now face a torture charge in addition to drug trafficking and gun counts.
Here's NPR's Ryan Lucas.
Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Celia Flores Maduro, have been in U.S. custody since they
were captured in an American military raid in January.
The Maduros were charged with narco-terrorism, drug and weapons offenses for allegedly working
with drug cartels to traffic cocaine to the United States.
They have pleaded not guilty.
Now they are facing one additional charge of torture.
Prosecutors allege Maduro used violence, including torture, to maintain power in Venezuela.
The alleged abuse included electric shock, rape, starvation and threats to kill victims'
families.
Prosecutors say U.S. citizens were among those subjected to such measures.
The couple is scheduled to go on trial in June.
That's Ryan Lucas reporting.
The administration laid out new plans to study the safety of vaccines.
Here's NPR's Rob Stein.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the opening of a new clinic at the National
Institutes of Health to study vaccine risks and how to treat people who experience complications.
He also announced plans to compensate doctors for reporting problems, require electronic
health records to include adverse reactions related to vaccines, and modernize the government
system for tracking problems.
Many vaccine experts say more research on vaccine safety is welcome, but there is overwhelming
evidence that the benefits of vaccines outweigh any rare risks.
They worry the new steps are just the latest effort by Kennedy to undermine confidence
and access to vaccines.
Rob Stein reporting.
It's NPR.
Britain and Israel have announced that the nearly 200-year-old British mission in Jerusalem
will stay open.
It will stay open with a different name and smaller scale.
That's after Israel had ordered the consulate to shut down in a dispute between the two
countries over sanctions, and NPR's Kat Lonsdorf has more from Tel Aviv.
The rift began last month after the UK ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied
West Bank and said that Israeli settlers are carrying out "ethnic cleansing" in the Palestinian
territory.
Israel responded by saying it would close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
After a discussion between the two countries, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced
that the building will stay open under a different name, the UK Mission Jerusalem, and a small
number of diplomats will remain.
Britain had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats if the consulate was closed.
Miliband said that won't happen for now.
It signals a deepening fracture in the relationship between the two countries, which until recently
had long been diplomatic allies.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
After nearly eight months in space, the four members of NASA's Crew-12 mission are back
home.
And as you can see on your screen, we have visual confirmation of splashdown.
SpaceX's livestream as a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule splashed down the Pacific Ocean off
the coast of Los Angeles, California today.
The two NASA astronauts, one from the European Space Agency and a Russian cosmonaut, spent
235 days aboard the International Space Station, a total of 237 days in space.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Hurricane East IES approaching Gulf Coast prompts evacuations and school closures Friday
Federal judge to decide by Tuesday on restoring White House press access for Politico, CNN, MSNow
Justice Department indicts former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and wife on torture charges
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announces new vaccine safety research clinic at NIH
Britain and Israel announce British mission in Jerusalem will remain open under new name
